newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Former Argentine minister alleges unethical donations.
newsitem.headline: Former Argentine minister alleges unethical donations.

text.p: A former Argentine economy minister on Friday charged that President Carlos Menem's aides accepted millions of dollars in campaign funds from Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi and an alleged mobster.

Domingo Cavallo, who has led a high-profile anti-corruption drive since he was fired from the government a year ago, told reporters Menem was not personally aware of the contributions and that Menem or other officials took actions to correct them once they were known.

The former "super minister" told a news conference Gaddafi paid $4 million to unidentified Menem aides in exchange for a promise to sell Libya Argentine Condor missiles. Cavallo, promoting his book "The Burden of Truth," said Menem scrapped the Condor project after Gaddafi himself informed him about the campaign contribution when they met in Belgrade in 1989.

"It looks like the boys sold the Condor to Gaddafi for an electoral campaign contribution," Cavallo quoted Menem as telling him immediately after meeting the Libyan leader. "How irresponsible! Now I am definitely convinced that we have to cancel the project as soon as possible."

Cavallo, who will run in mid-term congressional elections in October, told reporters he did not know whether Gaddafi's contribution was returned. He said the contributions were not illegal but suggested they were unethical.

A presidential spokesman, asked to comment, described Cavallo as a "big liar" whose accusations were motivated by his own bid to be elected this October. But the spokesman said he was unaware of the specific incidents raised by Cavallo, a Harvard-trained economist who was dismissed last July in a policy dispute with other ministers and ruling party members.

In his book, Cavallo said former Menem chief of staff Eduardo Bauza told him an Argentine tycoon who is now being investigated by a congressional anti-mafia committee had contributed $4 million to Menem's campaign to change the constitution to allow him to seek re-election.
The tycoon, Alfredo Yabran, is under investigation by the congressional committee and by police in their probe into who ordered the brutal murder of a news photographer last January.

Cavallo alleges the money was in exchange for a bill that would help Yabran take control of the mail service after its privatisation. He said Bauza agreed the move was "immoral" and pledged to return the money and fire the official who took it.
